segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As this year comes to an end, and we think about what politics looks like right now in our country, a good place to understand it is a state political party that made a very bold choice this year.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [GAVEL STRIKES]

segments.speaker: Dave Dishaw
segments.text: The convention will come to order.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The state is Michigan. This is a meeting that happened in February, where the Michigan Republican Party had to pick a new leader.

segments.speaker: Dave Dishaw
segments.text: If you want to return to your seats, you're welcome to. If you don't, that's fine. I know you're going to get up and sprint to vote here in a minute.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They were at a crossroads. They'd gotten killed in the midterm elections, which was just a few months before this-- creamed. They were further out of power than they'd been in 40 years, with Democrats controlling the State House, the Senate, the Governor's Office, most of the Congressional seats.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And why? Well, a big reason was because the Republicans had all these candidates who were pushing the idea that the presidential election had been stolen. And Michigan voters are not into that. They do not want to elect candidates who are obsessed with the election being stolen, apparently.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So at this meeting in February, the party needed to elect a leader who's going to rebuild and take the party forward. And if you think about it, one logical path they could have taken is, they could have picked somebody who renounced the whole election fraud thing. Right? All the conspiracy theories about voting machines and just all that stuff that Michigan voters are rejecting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But there were no candidates like that at all, nobody who said, let's drop all this election fraud stuff. Because a candidate like that would not have a ghost of a chance with the Republicans in this room, who are the ones who actually pick the new party leader. In the last few years, election-fraud stop-the-steal enthusiasts have driven out the regular, old-fashioned conservatives, and even other MAGA-loving Trump enthusiasts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Those people have been ousted, if they didn't care enough about election fraud or if they have ties to the old party establishment that this new guard sees as completely corrupt, compromising RINOs. So in the end, at this convention, there were nine candidates. And just to give you a sense of the range of this group, the most traditional Republican of this bunch was a guy named Scott Greenlee.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he's somebody who thought like, OK, election fraud is a problem. But he also came with connections to donors, to old-school pre-January 6 Republicans. In fact, Greenlee's an experienced political consultant, which, by the way, in this crowd, is not an asset. He talked to one of the producers on our show, Zoe Chace.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So everyone's telling me that you're the establishment candidate.

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: Oh, my goodness. Well, I get called all the names. I mean, I'm called establishment. I get called a RINO. That's even worse. I've also been called an "America First" guy, because in 2016, I was working extremely hard for President Trump, long before a lot of people were involved in the party.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So that's Scott Greenlee, the most traditional Republican. The least traditional candidate for party chair was a complete political outsider in every way, somebody whose involvement in politics started in 2020 as a poll watcher in Detroit, someone who got famous when she claimed that she saw election fraud with her own eyes. She went on to Steve Bannon's podcast and all kinds of right-wing media, and then ran for Secretary of State.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She's an arresting talker, Black, a Millennial, a devout Christian, named Kristina Karamo. So she tries to become Michigan Secretary of State and was soundly rejected by voters, defeated by 14 percentage points-- again, because Michigan voters are not going for the kind of election-fraud stuff that she was peddling. And she did not concede the race, still hasn't, which is something that the Republican delegates at the state convention loved about her.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: It's the reason I did not concede after the 2022 election. Why would I concede to a fraudulent process? Conceding to a fraudulent process is an agreement with the fraud, is which I will not do.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: We will grow this party without compromising our values. We're going to be a party that grows like never before. We're going to be a political machine that strikes fear in the heart of Democrats, and we're going to win. Vote Karamo Pego!

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: [CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And-- maybe you saw this coming-- Karamo wins. She becomes the head of the Michigan Republican Party, the outsiderist, the grassroots-ist-- not for nothing, the Christianist. And in picking Karamo, Michigan Republicans were saying, basically, what we want as a party is somebody to lead, who, A, believes the election was stolen, and B, has no connection to any establishment political machinery of the past, which is all corrupt.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That kind of purity test is something that you see a lot among Republicans right now. In the House of Representatives in Washington, so many political fights are basically between Republicans who don't want to compromise at all, and everybody else. You see this in other Republican state parties in swing states-- Arizona, Colorado, Georgia. But no state party has taken the flying leap off the cliff that the Michigan Republicans have.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: More than any other state party, they have the least politically connected, furthest-from-the-establishment, most ideological party leader and her followers running things. Among other things, I have to say it is an enormously idealistic act, done by true believers who feel deeply that the only way out of the mess that we're in as a country is a total break with what has come before. And when Karamo won, they were amped.

segments.speaker: Man 1
segments.text: I am excited. Everything's going to change.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There were tears.

segments.speaker: Woman 1
segments.text: (CRYING) Oh, my God!

segments.speaker: Woman 2
segments.text: Pray for her now. Now, it starts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today, on our program, when a political party takes a leap like this one, throws itself out in an act of faith like this one, in a major swing state, what does that gamble look like? What happens next? Today, we're going to look at how this year unfolded for these true believers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Producer Zoe Chace went many, many times to Michigan throughout this year and has a special up-close and personal look at how all this played out. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, The Lonely Island. OK, before we jump any deeper into this, maybe I should take a sec and explain just what a state party actually does. It's basically an organization set up to handle all kinds of boring, practical work that you need to do if you want to win elections. They recruit candidates. They organize meetings. There are these massive get-out-the-vote operations for state elections and for national candidates, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And above all else, they raise money to pay for campaigns, buy ads, and do everything else. And the person who raises that money, usually, is the party chair. So to have somebody with no political connections in that job like Kristina Karamo-- that is very unusual. Zoe tells the story from here.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Now, Kristina Karamo was elected in February, and the party did not pull together behind their new chair. There was a ton of infighting still over the first few months. And the first major test of her leadership, her ability to get things done, came this fall-- the Mackinac Island conference.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: It's a big, symbolic, fabled event in Michigan politics. Politicians, lobbyists, presidential candidates all make their way up to Northern Michigan and get on a ferry to this island where no cars are allowed-- horse-drawn carriages instead. So the whole place does smell like horse shit, which makes it a perfect setting for a group of politicos.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: They hobnob. They gossip. They make deals. They raise money. And the test for Kristina was, with all the old-school Republicans she and her followers have ejected from the party, could she raise enough money to even hold the conference? Would it even happen?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Raising money is probably the most important thing the state party chair does, and Kristina has no fundraising background. Over the last 10 years, the list of reported jobs she's done are the scraping-by kind-- salesclerk, trivia host, substitute teacher, adjunct community college instructor. She made a Christian podcast.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Her plan to fund the party was to get donations from small Republican businesses who have supposedly been sitting on the sidelines because they didn't think the party was conservative enough. But that never seemed to get off the ground. And for months before Mackinac, there were rumors like, how would she ever come up with the cash for this big showboaty affair?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: To get a read on those rumors, I checked in now and then with Jon Smith. He's the perfect person to go to, because he totally epitomizes what the Michigan GOP has become. He's an unabashed conspiracy theorist.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He started in state politics around 2020. He chartered two buses to get to January 6-- didn't go inside the Capitol, he says. And he and others stop-the-steal-ers took over their local county parties. Jon's on the state committee now. And he was like, I doubt Kristina raised enough money to pull off Mackinac.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I think they're lying to people about speakers and stuff. They don't have a way to pay for them, I don't think. But I think-- you know that documentary with that guy that did that concert on the island-- "Fry"? I think that's what they're doing here.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: [LAUGHS] The Fyre Festival.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: But it's MIGOP, you know. That's what District 9 chair is telling me.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Literally, in the Fyre Festival documentary, people show up in the Bahamas, and instead of Blink 182 and the Instagram models they were promised, there is no music, no food, no water, and soggy FEMA tents. What we all find at Mackinac isn't quite that desperate.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: [PIANO PLAYING]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: When I got up to the Grand Hotel, there was definitely a Republican conference taking place, with Trump hats and red-white-and-blue sparkly pins, as promised. And a grand piano playing a song about how anything is possible if only you believe.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But apparently, this year was really different from past years. At night, I was wandering with a couple attendees, including one of the younger vice chairs, Hassan Nehme, in a suit and a low founding-fathers-y ponytail. We were headed upstairs in an elevator, looking for the Mackinac parties, which I'd heard were legendary.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Oh, you haven't been to one of these before?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Oh, yeah, it's very fun.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: This is your first time in Mackinac.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Oh, yeah, this is very-- it's like-- imagine going to the mall, and there's, like, one store open. This is how this weekend feels to me.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: In what way? How is it like one store--

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: 'Cause last time you walk on the porch, there's, like, 800 people, and now, there's, like, nobody--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: --in every event.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yeah. Last time, there were around 2,000 attendees. This year, the best guess I saw was 800 at the very most. Last time, Ted Cruz was a keynote speaker. A big name national Republican. This time? QAnon proponent Jim Caviezel, who made the sleeper summer hit movie about child sex trafficking, Sound of Freedom. He also played Jesus in the Passion of the Christ.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Out on the colossal porch at one point, I talked to another state committee member who was upset about how things seemed to be going.

segments.speaker: Mark Forton
segments.text: Well, it's not exactly what we were hoping or anticipating.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Mark Forton is one of those who wanted a complete break with how it used to be. And how it used to be was that the head of the party was a super-rich Michigan guy, real estate mogul Ron Weiser. In the last few years, the party yearly budget has been something like $20 million, a chunk of which came directly from Weiser, and mostly one other rich family in Michigan-- the Devoses.

segments.speaker: Mark Forton
segments.text: We knew that if the grassroots took over the state party, that the big shooters would go. Not all of them, but we knew the DeVos family would go and Mr. Weiser would go. They're all globalist. They're all part of the same great, big mess that Michigan's in-- you know, bringing in the Chinese, battery factories. So I mean, we know they're globalists.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And then, Mark spins out the first of the many times I will hear the theory that Kristina is a globalist plant, and that the reason things are going so badly is that the establishment planned it this way, from the beginning of her rise to power.

segments.speaker: Mark Forton
segments.text: They knew the grassroots had had enough and they're going to take over this party. They knew it then. Now, the question is, are these globalist types-- are they going to sit by and take it? Or are they going to start planning for when the grassroots take over-- what do we do next? They're after Michigan. There's no doubt.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But she's like the most anti-globalist of them all. She's the anti-globalistest.

segments.speaker: Mark Forton
segments.text: Oh, I know. I'm not accusing her. I'm saying, but who's pulling the strings? Who-- I just don't know what to think. I'm telling you things that-- you're asking me what's on my mind.

segments.speaker: Mark Forton
segments.text: You're asking me what I'm concerned about. And none of them are facts. But my gosh, you look at all this crap going on, and you can't come up with a decent answer. I just don't know. I just-- I'm trying to find out.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: That's not the only conspiracy theory I hear about Kristina. In the hallway, I run into someone whose conspiracy theory is on a parallel track, but going the other way-- Braden Giacobazzi, kind of a frantic little dude. He's a major Kristina supporter, a chair on one of her committees.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Braden says it's not Kristina who's the globalist plant. Instead, there are secret operatives within the party who are trying to take her out. They're doing it by starting all these rumors. He and his friend, Ken Beyer, another Karamo loyalist, told me about a few.

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: Like, today, they came up with a rumor that Karamo is going to retire. It's, like, the most absurd nonsense.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I saw that on Twitter.

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: But why even start that rumor? What is that?

segments.speaker: Ken Beyer
segments.text: They lied, because they didn't want people to show up and pack the house. That's why they didn't--

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: That's exactly what they did.

segments.speaker: Ken Beyer
segments.text: So they-- I mean, we've been fighting this for a while, and all they do is lie, lie, lie, lie, lie, lie, lie.

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: And they'll make up the most absurd rumors, because they know if they do that, it'll make-- it will try to discredit this event, try to discredit the administration, and try to discredit, basically, all of the MIGOP.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Why would they want to do that?

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: People want power. There's an old saying. I don't know where it comes from. But some people would rather rule over ashes than allow somebody to beat them.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: Right?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: --something Kristina Karamo said.

segments.speaker: Braden Giacobazzi
segments.text: That's absolutely-- oh, well, there you go. I think it's from Game of Thrones.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The actual business at Mackinac, the meeting of party leaders, was a showdown between Kristina supporters and Kristina skeptics about party finances. This was a closed meeting, but I got a tape. Kristina's team claimed they'd raised $650,000. The skeptics demanded they open up the books and prove it. Toward the end of the meeting, Kristina went to the podium to defend herself.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: As far as the financial health of the party, the party is not going bankrupt. It's not. But-- but-- but I mean, what-- if you received the treasurer report, unless you think the treasurer is lying to you-- now, I will make a comment about a lot of the people who aren't giving. Is it because they don't like or feel we're going to bankrupt or because they don't like the philosophical direction of the party?

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: That's what's really going on here.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: At the end of the day, Kristina's team does not agree to, quote unquote, "open the books," show them the party finances. And everyone trudges down to the boats, frustrated with each other, dodging the piles of fresh horse shit.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Act Two, Another Purity Test. Just a few days after the conference ended, there was something else, that really has nothing to do with money, that came up about Kristina's GOP-- about who's welcome inside this party. It was an email anonymously penned by a guy who called himself Paul Revere.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And the gist was, an Islamic takeover of America is happening. Homicidal Islamic terrorists are becoming entrenched and infecting our whole country. It concluded, "To paraphrase Sir Winston Churchill, Islam in a man is as dangerous as rabies in a dog."

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: This email was sent out to district chairs and vice chairs of the state party. Three of the vice chairs are Muslim, and two of them replied all, because they felt attacked by the anonymous email. One of them was Hassan Nehme, the guy I was in the elevator with at Mackinac. Here's what he wrote.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: "Good evening, Kristina. This email was sent out to the Republican leadership, every elected member, and all the district chairs. Conveniently, you were not added, So I decided to forward it over. I noticed that others have forwarded it to you, so I was eagerly awaiting a response from you."

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Hassan wants her to condemn it publicly. He continues, "I took the liberty of reaching out to my contacts at Fox, ABC, and a couple of the Detroit news outlets today, with the hopes that you would join the Muslim vice-chairs to respond to this. We need to ensure our constituents understand that the party will not stand for this and that our party stands for the Constitution, which defends the freedom of religion.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So you either join us on air and we all play nice and show what our party stands for, or we go on there and talk about how you have sidelined us and that you have yet to condemn any of this rhetoric." Hassan says he never heard back from Kristina.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I went to talk with Hassan and his cousin Ali about their place in the party, if there even is a place in this party for them under Karamo. These are idealistic Republicans who agree with her and what she stands for. They were like exactly what you might think the Republican Party would want-- young Muslim guys in the Democratic stronghold of Dearborn, genuinely excited about the potential of bringing Arab Americans into the Republican Party.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I met them at a business they own, a print shop in a cellar, no cell phone service, no windows, fluorescent lights, concrete walls, and their dog Pickles. Where we sat in the back was a big sign up for Hassan's election. He ran for the US House a year ago, for Rashida Tlaib's seat. Or he tried.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I didn't even make it past the primaries. It was-- I spent my entire campaign trying to prove to the Republicans that I was a Republican because of my faith, so it was very fun.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: What is that-- what was that like?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: It was very interesting. It was the first time my life I sat in a meeting where they're talking about anti-Sharia law. And I'm a Muslim. I didn't know what Sharia law was.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: So I'm just sitting there listening to these people talk things about my faith that I don't even believe, and how we're getting into politics to take it all over and corrupt society. And I'm just sitting there like-- I'm a politician, running for Congress, sitting in the audience, listening to this. And it happened a lot. It happened a lot. It's kind of what led to running for the vice-chair roles-- was kind of, hey, this is not right.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The more people seem to doubt them, the more these guys wanted to prove that they belonged. Like, we're family-values conservatives, too. We're concerned about what our kids are learning in schools, too. We think there's big election fraud, too. We belong here so much, we actually should be in the leadership of the party.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Hassan ran for coalitions vice chair, Ali ran for administrative vice chair. No one ran against them. Still, on the day of the leadership race, when Karamo was elected chair, one of the people in their own district tried to sabotage them.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: They wanted to open the floor to nominations, because they couldn't let the Muslims run unopposed. And there was ladies out of Macomb-- and this was, like-- a lot of people have on record, saying, like, they were going around saying those exact quotes.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Yeah, isn't that crazy?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: That's Ali, Hassan's cousin, admin vice chair. He's more relaxed than Hassan, tipped back in his seat. He says things started to get weird right before the vote.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: While right before that, some lady came up to us. I forgot her name, but she was talking to us like, hey, do you take Jesus Christ as your Lord and Savior? And we're like, bro, what the-- that's so off.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: That's out of pocket, first of all. Second of all, you're asking someone that doesn't believe in that if they want to believe in it now. Like, you didn't even build up to it.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: This is just like, you walked onto the convention floor--

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: I wouldn't hire her if I had a sales company.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: She came up to where our districts are. We were going to our district's areas. And it was just rude, the way--

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Yeah, it was so rude.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: And no, but we had the conversation-- I had the conversation with her gladly. And then actually, after the convention, I met up with her, and we had another conversation for, like, an hour. I'm more than willing to entertain that conversation, how our faiths are very similar or not.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I'm not an enemy. We are not enemies, the way the media perceives it. But I'll have that conversation all day, but--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Wait, tell the story, though. Because I feel like I'm missing the beginning of the story. So what happened?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: So we were at convention, doing our rounds. This is the day of the election, so we're talking to everybody, letting them know, hey, this is our plan. This is what we're doing. We're introducing ourselves. You know, yada, yada.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: And somebody goes up there during new business and wants to put it out there, like hey, we want to open the floor to have them-- or change bylaws so we could put people up against them. And everybody starts going crazy. And--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Did they say specifically, like, because they're Muslim?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Yeah, they were passing out pamphlets. We learned after the fact, that there were pamphlets being passed out by these ladies. Like, how are you going to let their voices-- and then--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Just to be clear, someone stood up during convention to make a motion that someone could declare their candidacy right then, to stop these Muslims from becoming leaders of the party. Still, it didn't pass, and these guys ended up as vice chairs. They were excited. Like, hey, what's my budget line? What's the credentials to start emailing people as official state party representatives?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Let's drive around, set up meetings, do whatever it is this new experimental group of people wants to do, to reach out to people. But there were no leadership team meetings. They say no one called them to tell them, here's what we want you to do and how to do it, and that they were the ones, Hassan and Ali, who set up the first leadership meeting for vice chairs all across the state. Kristina didn't show up to it.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Then, there was the whole Mackinac situation. The guys wanted to help plan it, and the bylaws say that the admin vice chair-- that's Ali-- is supposed to play a big role in planning it. But they say no one would communicate with them about it. Finally, they ended up at a meeting in Lansing with Kristina and some of her team, where they came away with the message, we don't want people like you leading things with this party.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: In Hassan and Ali's telling, this is how the meeting went. Hassan was like, why aren't you advertising what a diverse leadership we are? You're Black. You have three Arab-Muslim vice chairs. You have an Indian-American district chair. You should be talking about that.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Yeah, it all goes back to, it's a Judeo-Christian movement, and somehow, my faith doesn't play a role in that.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: This was said to you explicitly?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Well, yeah, along those lines. You want exact-- but yes, along those lines, it's like, it's the Judeo-Christian values, and we're not a part of this plan.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: How did it make you feel?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I don't know. I'm used to it. I don't care. I'm still going to do what I think is right.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You must have been upset, hurt.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: It just bothers you, because it's not like-- the Federalist Papers and the Anti-Federalist Papers were some of the best things I've ever read in my life, and those conversations that took place. And then, you deal with this type of rhetoric, and you're like, if we're truly talking about the founding fathers, the founding fathers did all of this so there's freedom of religion, so--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Ali had stepped out and walks back into the room at this point.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: What did you say, Hassan? Let me see--

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: No, we were talking about the diversity and why we're not playing it and playing the three--

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Oh, yeah, yeah. She said--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: "She," Kristina.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: The country wasn't founded off of Muslim beliefs. It was founded off of Judeo-Christian beliefs. And that's a fact. You can look that up for yourself." And then, I'm like, yeah, we understand that, but like, let's be more inclusive and word it differently, so everyone's included, you know. Because we got the most amount of Muslims in America right in your-- like, right there, you know?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I don't want to talk about what was said in that conversation, like exactly what was said.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Yeah, don't-- be nice about everything.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Hassan starts to get annoyed, staring down the table at Ali.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: But yeah, she was--

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: No, I'm genuinely-- we're trying to keep our Republican Party together, and I'm not-- this just makes it a lot more--

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Hey, the truth is the truth, man. Once you say something, you say it.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I'm not against the truth, man. I'm not against the truth. It's just, this would cause much more problems when it comes out-- the wording that was used-- it plays the rhetoric-- then hey, we were just told that you guys are not a part of the plan.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Well, she didn't say that.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Basically, they felt like at the meeting in Lansing, that they were being subjected to a different purity test-- not one about who was grassroots enough, but about whether anybody but Christians had a place in Kristina Karamo's party. I talked to Kristina about this, and she categorically denied this version of events. She says, of course, there's a place for Muslims in her leadership, and she says she did try to include Hassan and Ali, but they were unresponsive.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Hassan shared screenshots with me that showed him reaching out to her about Mackinac specifically and getting brushed off. In any case, by the time they got to Mackinac, which they had played no part in putting together, Hassan and Ali were feeling salty.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: We got there, and we didn't even-- they didn't even make us name tags. And that was a statement. Like, you already know--

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: That was so mean.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: That was offensive. And they got mad when we asked, where's our name tags? Like, hey, guys, we don't have name tags, and they're like, here, and then they gave us, like-- whatever. At that point, I'm not going to lie, I was kind of being petty.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: They gave us, like, General Admission, and I'm like, hey, we're vice chairs. Like, no, no, no. Can I get a VIP one? Like, what are you guys doing?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: But yeah, we were not involved. All I did there to help was, during the meeting on Sunday, the lights guy asked me if he could head out, so I told him, yeah, go ahead, leave. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Nice.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: We're still talking when Hassan's phone rings. It's Jon Smith, the guy I always talk to about what's happening in the party-- the Fyre Festival guy. He's got news.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Hey, did you guys see McCarthy today?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: No, I've been doing a six-hour-long interview.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Did you see-- did you see, Zoe?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: No, I've been in the interview, too.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: So, so Matt Gaetz led the charge, and they got McCarthy out and voted with the Democrats.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Oh, they got him out?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He's out?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: First time in history.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Relatable to these new Michigan Republicans, who have a habit of overthrowing. First, they overthrew their own establishment. Now, they're having buyer's remorse over the bet they made on Kristina, wondering if they should try to remove her, too.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I mean, there's no good time to remove a leadership role. But if it's out of spite, then I don't like it. If it's out of principle and it's true to what they're saying, then fuck it, go for it.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: You know, I kind of agree with Jon there. Like, if everything is really as corrupt as they're saying and we get more solid evidence, and everything's spread to the light and it looks like what it is, then I don't see these efforts as being misguided.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Are you talking about Kristina now or are you still talking about McCarthy?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I was ordering pizza, so I just jumped in, pretending I know what we were talking about, to be honest. So were we talking about Kristina or McCarthy right now?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But as far as Jon Smith personally goes, he buried the lead on this call. Hassan checks his email while we're on the phone.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: "Jon Smith's resignation"? Jon Smith.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: As district chair?

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Jon? What are you thinking, man?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I'm trying to understand why you decided to resign.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I can't-- I can't afford to play the game anymore.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: What are you going to--

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: It's an expensive hobby.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: What are you going to do for work?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Construction work.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: I'm hiring.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: So I quit, because I can't afford to play, man. It's expensive, going across the district, you know? And it's just, uh-- it's hard on the bank, man. To be honest with you, I wake up to politics 24/7. So I mean, I need to get off the mindset and get into work.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: I mean, I'm right there with you, man. It's--

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I drive a 2000 Saturn with one fender, guys.

segments.speaker: Hassan Nehme
segments.text: Hey. I mean, I put 90,000 miles on my truck, and I was forced to buy my lease because of this, and spent a lot of-- I promise you, I'm in the same boat, and it's-- ugh. But I'm just hoping we-- you know, it works.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: It doesn't-- it doesn't-- it's not working out. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: That is an interesting question to me. These leadership roles are volunteer, not paid. Like, did the party only work before because there were rich people who could afford to do them?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: How long can the not-rich people afford to be in political leadership here? Of all the people to leave now, I'm surprised it's Jon. You know, he was one of the first people in Michigan to make a show of pushing out the establishment-- part of this wave of new leaders who ousted their county chairs to create this grassroots state party, run by the newbies, disconnected from the old guard. He walked so Kristina could run.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: As for Hassan and Ali, they hadn't found the party an especially welcoming place, either before or after Kristina's takeover. But they're going to keep trying. Seeing how hard they're having to fight to be included, it makes me think about how relatively unimportant winning seems to be in post-January 6 purity politics.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Like, if the party wanted to win, you could imagine a world where they'd be reaching out to guys like this instead of sidelining them. But instead, it seems that this new version of the party is winnowing it down to a relatively small, untainted-by-compromise group of principled people. Not a winning strategy for a political party-- in Michigan in particular.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Zoe Chace. Coming up, how to topple a Republican leader? Well, like somebody said a half-century ago, follow the money. It's about to get real. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. As this year ends, noticing the kind of fights happening among Republicans in the US House of Representatives and around the country, we have this political story that we thought captures something about the state of Republican politics this year from Michigan. We're calling the episode, "It Wouldn't Be Make Believe if You'd Believe in Me." Zoe Chace picks up where she left off.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The last week of September, the plot to oust Kristina heated up, when someone in the Michigan GOP sent out a barrage of screenshots to a few reporters. They were of bank statements of the Michigan GOP. It was a little confusing, this collection of random screenshots, but it did seem like the party was almost completely out of money.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Jon Smith got the texts. He didn't see any evidence of this thing Kristina's people had said at Mackinac about the money they'd raised. He was depressed.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: And they just told us we raised $600,000, which is a lie. They're lying, Zoe. They're lying. They're lying to everyone.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I guess, do you think they're lying because they're, like, corrupt? Or do you think they're lying because they're scared?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I think they're scared. That's what I'm saying. We would be OK with it if they would just open the books. We would help them. If we need to raise $150,000 this weekend, we would all go out as a united front across the state of Michigan and make it happen. They're choosing to be deceptive.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Like, you think that if from the very beginning they had said, hey, we're not going to any of the old donors, we're doing a whole new thing, so we need you guys to fundraise, like, all the time, people would have gone with that?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I don't know. But they could have just been honest right from the get-go.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You don't feel bad leaving people kind of in the middle of this mess?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: No, I can't, Zoe. I got to go to work.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: People were getting scared that the party was in no way going to be able to run next year's elections. There would be no fundraising, no Get Out the Vote, no coordination of strategy. They were going to lose control of 2024. And that brings us to Act 3, "The Insurrectionists Insurrect Again."

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The guy who leaked the bank account screenshots-- Warren Carpenter-- was a major Kristina supporter at first. Warren helped get Kristina elected. He raised money for her secretary-of-state campaign. He whipped votes for her chair race.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I went to talk to him. He runs a landscaping business in the suburbs of Detroit. He walked me to the back of his office.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: This is uncomfortable.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Is it?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah. I don't like it.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You'll get used to it.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Ah, I don't like it. I don't want to do that. You want to record me?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Well, it's radio. That's why.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: [SIGHS]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Warren comes off antagonistic right from the beginning, and a little manic. What he's just done-- leaking documents to the press about Kristina-- it's a big deal, though.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: How are you? You got a lot going on?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Well-- [LAUGHS] It's like you didn't read the news or something.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: "It's like you didn't read the news or something," he says. That morning, the morning we spoke, September 29, Detroit News reporter Craig Mauger, an eminently fair and lightning-fast journalist, published a write-up of all the documents Warren had sent him.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The article begins, "The Michigan Republican Party had about $35,000 in its bank account in August, according to internal records that flashed new warning signs about the dire state of the GOP's finances." This is followed shortly by a quote from a former state GOP official-- "These numbers demonstrate that the party isn't just broke, but broken."

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Warren is also extensively quoted in the article, which is a big betrayal of Kristina, talking to a journalist who, in her view, is just in league with the establishment trying to take her out. Warren says he dabbled in Republican politics before this movement took off, worked on a statewide campaign over 10 years ago, but not much since then, until Trump.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He loves Trump, calls him Big Daddy, and had that school board come-to-Jesus so many Republicans did around the COVID protocols-- masking in schools kind of thing. He went to January 6 after he thought he saw the election get stolen. Says he didn't go inside the Capitol, but he had such an intense experience there, that not long after, he had a mental breakdown, as he puts it.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: That's when he got involved in his local party. He's one of the newbies who got elected to district chair, part of the wave that took over the party this year. He'd been part of Kristina's inner circle, but now, he'd resigned from his position as district chair and was talking smack in the press. So what happened?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Well, a few weeks before the Mackinac conference, Warren got on the phone with Kristina's chief of staff, Joel Studebaker, and the rest of her team. And they were telling him they needed help to pull off the conference. So he looked at their financial situation, and he responded with what I now understand to be his typical intensity.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: How much money do you have? How much money do we need? How much money are we owed? Who's been paid? Right?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: What's the problem? What do you need? Why am I on the fucking call with you? But like, Joel Studebaker didn't know what the numbers were.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Like, they didn't know any of the numbers for anything. They were literally flying by the fucking seat of their pants, shooting from the hip. It was-- I mean, it was the most ludicrous thing I've ever heard of in my entire life.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Like, there was no budgetary schematic they could share with me. And during that initial Friday call, the only thing they had to share was like, they almost had the program ready to go to the printer.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: A program with speakers on it they didn't have the cash to pay for, it seemed. Warren called campaign finance experts, who looked at what he had and told him to get as far away as possible from this organization.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I've looked at Warren's documents, and what I saw looked like a broke party, spending money way faster than it was taking anything in. I also went over the party's FEC filings, though they haven't filed since July. In all that I looked at, I did see some very unusual accounting, but nothing illegal, like Warren alleges.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: So there's only two ways that this could-- there's only two things that this could possibly be, in my mind, all right? It is either gross negligence, incompetence, right? I would ascribe intent and say that it's malicious. And therefore, if it's malicious, then you have to go to the next conclusion, which is, then it's destruction of the party. Now, can you ascribe intent for destruction of the party?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Warren goes on to float his own version of the sabotage theory I heard from other people, that Kristina herself is controlled by some kind of national operation, launched at the Michigan Republican Party in order to destroy it.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Either an operative or it's a fed. But it's either from the Democratic side or it's from an agency.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He's pretty sure it's an op and that it's not just in Michigan. That would explain why GOPs in Georgia, Arizona, and Idaho are struggling. Someone's sabotaging them. But even if it's not an op, as someone who helped put Kristina in office in the first place, Warren now feels responsible for where she's brought the party.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And Warren's a doer. He's also make-amends-er. I find that out myself when he calls me and apologizes for yelling at me at one point. Maybe that comes from his years in AA.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So Warren has a plan to make things right. Oust Kristina Karamo. He has a whole 18-point plan to do it. That Detroit News article was a first step. Now he's whipping votes against her, just like he whipped votes for her at the beginning of the year, trying to make sure he has the numbers.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: You file for the meeting. When we get the signatures, we're going to have all the signatures needed to overthrow. So then it just shows them, it's over. I want psychologically for them to be beat before they even go into this. And it's over.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Uh, OK, everybody, I just want to get started real quick about why everyone's on the phone call.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: The next time I hear Warren's voice, it's from a Zoom meeting someone sent me of state committee members from around Michigan. Warren called the meeting. He has a spreadsheet of the 100-or-so people in the state committee color-coded-- who's with him, who's against him. He's literally counting votes, trying to get to that majority to oust Kristina.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: OK, so let's go through this real quick. Everybody in red is in red until they're probably confirmed otherwise. So I need some people to speak up as we go through some of these. I mean, Andy, is there anybody in your district that's not on board with this? Andy? You muted? All right.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: No, they're all-- all those people are for this.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: That's not Andy. That's Jon Smith. Despite having quit as district chair, he can't stay away. Warren and Jon go back and forth on whether or not they have a 2/3 majority. Or do they only need 50%?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Listen, if we don't have enough, if we don't have 2/3, we don't call the fucking meeting. Right? Nancy Pelosi doesn't bring anything to the floor if it doesn't have all the fucking votes. Neither do I.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: So I mean, that's it right there. You got the 2/3 to call the meeting. It's over. I'm telling you. So let me just-- just trust me on this, please, guys. I know I'm forceful, and I'm sorry.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: I'm a boss, and nobody ever tells me no, and that's why I'm not good at this job. That's why I'm not a good district chair, and I'm not good at collaboration stuff. And please don't take my forcefulness for trying to beat up on anybody. It's not what I'm trying to do. I'm trying to convince you that this is a--

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Well, we're at the threshold of 50%. That's what I'm telling people when I'm talking to people is like, do we not move forward, or where do we get to the point where we have to start having this discussion? So I think we're at that point with 54 people. I mean, that's a significant number.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: That's more than 50%. We are the majority on state committee at this point without whipping a single fucking person.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Then who shows up in the Zoom? The guy Warren lined up to replace Karamo. And guess who it is? Scott Greenlee. Yes, Scott Greenlee, the guy who ran for chair from the beginning of the story, who wasn't America-first enough to get elected in the first place. Remember?

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: I'm called establishment. I get called a RINO. That's even worse.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Now, he makes his pitch to this renegade faction that he should be the choice of the renegade faction. And he cuts quickly to the chase.

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: I think I could probably raise $1/2 million in the first week, a couple million by the end of the year, 5 by March, and salvage the cycle with about $10 million in total fundraising. And certainly, we have the challenge that some people wouldn't like, necessarily, everyone who is donating to the party. But I would welcome any and all dollars, within reason.

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: I mean, certainly, if Hillary Clinton moved to Michigan and said she wanted to help, I'd be a little suspicious. But short of that, if people want to help this party rebuild, they're going to get an open door not a closed door.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Some donors won't come back, Greenlee says. It's going to be a hard sales job to go to people who've been demonized. Of course, I'll include grassroots, but we all got to play nice together. Warren interrupts him.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Hey, Scott. I had a question sent to me. How can you assure us that John Yob will not be running the party?

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: John Yob is a powerful political consultant in Michigan. He's been around, a political director for the John McCain campaign, symbol of the hated establishment.

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: Uh, because I'll be the chairman. I mean--

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Real questions, man. This is--

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Hey-- hey, Scott? Hey, Scott? This is Jon. That would be a real question. You know, you just said you have a hard time identifying what is grassroots and stuff like that. But that is a legit question.

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: Sure. So John and I have worked together. John and I have worked against each other. But you know, unless you guys are liking John Yob as chair, he's not running the party. I guarantee that. I'll take his input when it makes sense. That's for sure.

segments.speaker: Scott Greenlee
segments.text: I don't want to close anybody out. I don't want to manage by exclusion. I think we need everybody pushing in the same direction. But I will make the decisions the chairman needs to make. And you elect me, and I'll be running the party.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Greenlee-- from another era, it sounds like-- talking to consultants, raising money, being inclusive, bringing people in, instead of cutting people out. The call ends shortly after that. They don't quite have the numbers to oust Kristina. I can't tell how Greenlee went over. Jon's not sure either. He and Warren chat afterwards.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Hey, Warren.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: What up, Jonny?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I put Tom in the waiting room. What are you--

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: What'd you think?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Yeah, that's what I was going to ask you.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Uh, like, here's the thing.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Warren's moving a million miles an hour. He's like, Scott or not, I know I'm going to get the votes to remove her. Jon's still stuck on whether the grassroots will stomach him.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: I think he's an honest guy.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah, he's super honest, dude.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: You know what I mean? Like, if he says he's going to do it, I think he will do that.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah. Because there's a reason he's the only guy that's still allowed in all the rooms, dude. All the rest of these consultants are like ghosts. They're like vapors.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: You don't ever see 'em anywhere. They're always lurking. Like, he's out in the open every single day, like, posting on Facebook about how to be a good leader, dude. You know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Yeah. I'm wondering if Scott Greenlee is salvageable to the delegates. And I think he very well could be. It's not like we got that many options, though. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Hey, listen, my wife--

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Do your thing.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Night, brother.

segments.speaker: Jon Smith
segments.text: Good night.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Act Four, Karamo Fights Back.

segments.speaker: Darlene
segments.text: There's been a coup attempt to overthrow Kristina, and they've got a bunch of people that were lying. OK? You want to know some of the lies that were out there?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Darlene
segments.text: Oh, Kristina went to meet Donald Trump for dinner, and she came in a swimsuit and a cover-up.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: This is Darlene, Kristina supporter. I'm at a pasta dinner, called by Kristina's chief of staff, in a swanky ballroom in the suburbs of Detroit. The invitation read, "Join MIGOP Chief of Staff Joel Studebaker as he offers a rebuttal to claims of impropriety." In other words, spaghetti, meatballs, a PowerPoint for dessert. Darlene's here for it.

segments.speaker: Darlene
segments.text: All right? They're kind of manipulating things to where it looks one way. Kristina has not drawn a paycheck since July. All right?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You can see that in some of the filings.

segments.speaker: Darlene
segments.text: First of all, they said, oh, Mackinac is not going to happen. She's skimming the money. The speakers aren't getting paid. It's going to end up in the parking lot. Don't go. Refund your ticket. Mackinac was a huge success.

segments.speaker: Darlene
segments.text: Kristina went back to what a conference should be-- God, country, and party, and family. She went there. She didn't go with all the dinner parties, all the different drinking parties.

segments.speaker: Darlene
segments.text: She went to bring us all back to our roots. She is grassroots, and she's grassroots all the way. She is not selling out. She never has, and she never will.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Downstairs, in the room literally just below this one, in another giant ballroom, is Warren, sitting alone with his laptop, a projector behind him. He booked the room at 3:00 PM today, after he heard he was going to be barred from attending Kristina's rebuttal event. He's wearing a red baseball cap that says "Trump was right," and he's totally by himself.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Oh my gosh.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I was like, is it him? How are you doing, man?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Come on in.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Hi. So?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: What's up?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I don't know. Does it feel weird, everybody upstairs and you down here?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Swear to God, dude.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Because I know, like, you lost all your friends, and that must feel hard.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Oh, are we doing the thing right now?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I'm always recording.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: OK, well, I don't know, man. You come over with the microphone, I'm not sure.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Sorry.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: It's taking Warren longer than he expected to execute his 18-point plan. Because, as he says, he's a vote counter, and he hasn't been getting enough people on the board. And last week, he got invited to a meeting of the Macomb County GOP to present his documents and make his case.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: He put up a rapidfire slideshow for the delegates to convince them that Kristina was a fraud. And honestly, he sounded slightly unhinged. Here's some Facebook video of that event.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Guess what? There's more! There's another one! Wait! There's four more! Over $100,000 that can't be accounted for in deposits! (YELLING) This is your party!

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But he's raised enough heat that Karamo's people decided they want to respond publicly to his claims. Hence the pasta dinner and counterpresentation. For Warren's part, he's here to respond to the response to his claims and try to keep his cool.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: My whole motive of coming tonight was I'm just going to be calm.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Right? And I was going to answer people's questions if they had concerns. And--

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: Are you in the middle of an interview?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Someone comes in and asks, are you in the middle of an interview?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah, she's talking to me just real quick. But do you want to talk?

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: I just wanted to bring her up to speed on what's going on down here. Can you give her a kind of an overview?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah. So anybody that wants to ask anything after all this is done, they come down here, and I'll open up documents, show them whatever they want to see.

segments.speaker: Woman 3
segments.text: Are they the same documents you put up?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: I got everything-- I got everything that I got.

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: If you had pasta, I'd stay.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Then it would-- I get it, I get it.

segments.speaker: Man 2
segments.text: You gotta spend the money.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You got some curious customers.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: In the ballroom upstairs, it's maybe 75 people. Kristina's chief of staff, Joel Studebaker, is presenting a rebuttal to Warren's crazed Facebook video. He opens with a Bible verse, but then gets surprisingly detailed, shows snapshots of bank statements. After complaining that the previous administration left them with little money and some debt, which is true, there's this admission.

segments.speaker: Joel Studebaker
segments.text: Here's the reality. Fundraising has been a challenge. It's been very difficult. A lot of these things, you know, they're just realities. And we need help. We do need help.

segments.speaker: Joel Studebaker
segments.text: But you got to be able to work together. And there's no way we're going to do that if we keep giving liberal media interviews and if we keep walking through demonization schemes. It's just not going to happen. So we need help, and we need to do it the right way. We need to collaborate.

segments.speaker: Woman 4
segments.text: Yes, we do. Yes!

segments.speaker: Woman 4
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: When Kristina finally speaks, she talks about finances, about Mackinac, and she's frank. She admits they would have liked to make a lot more money off the conference. They're still in debt for $110,000 speaker's fee-- for Jim Caviezel, for example.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: She reminds everyone that the reason they elected her is they wanted to run the party differently, not raise $20 million and run right through it like previous chairs.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: So where did all this $20 million go? What was it spent on? Oh, I know, a bunch of consultants who did nothing. So that's what it was spent on.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: I mean, where did all the money get-- people brag about how much money they raised, and then go pay off their friends. So that what's been going on for decades. So yes, we disrupted that system. So you know--

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: She spoke for 20 minutes, no pauses or hesitations, mostly informing the crowd of mostly supporters that she was the victim of a deep-state conspiracy to take her out.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: Again, this whole deep-state thing is very real. It is very real. Because their goal is that if these people don't succeed, not just here, but also places like Colorado, Kansas, Georgia, where you have a bunch of America-first chairs, the goal for these people is, if these people fail, then a grassroots person won't dare run for chair.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: And a lot of the people who may or may not want to support a grassroots person for chair wouldn't do it because it's like, well, last time, it was so horrible. We can never do it again.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: She called out the people she sees as covert deep-state operatives within the current party. When she describes them, they sound a lot like Warren.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: And the thing about it is, these people-- they pretend to be patriots like us so they can get close to us. They pretend to be one of us so we will trust them.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Moving on next to Ali and Hassan, not by name.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: I mean, I had two vice chairs falsely accuse me of being a bigot against Muslims.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But she insists, her administration hasn't ever lied or committed any crimes. The fighting itself, she says, is a tactic to keep her from succeeding. The fighting, however, immediately continues.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Back downstairs in Warren's room, a guy from Kristina's team swaggers in to confront Warren. His name's Ken Beyer. He said he'd received a text from Warren saying, I'm coming after you. Warren says, it just said, I'm coming. And there's this big Wild-West-y faceoff between them.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Hey, Ken! You going to ask some questions?

segments.speaker: Ken Beyer
segments.text: Oh, I just [INAUDIBLE]. If you're going to threaten me, do it to my face.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Oh, I'd never threaten you at all. Get out of here. Listen, I could have you removed for trespassing, just as you were about to have me removed. I didn't threaten you. It wasn't ever a threaten.

segments.speaker: Ken Beyer
segments.text: But if you want to threaten me, do it to my face.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: I never threatened you, Ken. You seem like you're upset. Good night.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Now, a little crowd gathers, watching them go at it across the basement ballroom.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Come on, Ken. Look at all the files, baby! Come on, baby, come on!

segments.speaker: Ken Beyer
segments.text: What about your felony?

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: Yeah, I got a felony for drunk driving. It was years ago. See this right here? That's a negative in the account! There's the $15,000 that came in!

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: This is the problem with the coup Warren's trying to pull off. It's the problem that was baked into Karamo's version of the party from the start. This group of people all agree on some basic issues-- election fraud, less immigration, no gun control, abortion is murder, don't tell me when to wear a mask, don't tell my children what to read, and the rent is too damn high.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But what's brought them all together running this party is their lack of trust in any kind of political leadership. They are a very suspicious, conspiracy-minded group. And that's how they look at everything, including each other. Of course they can't agree on who the real enemy is of the cause they all actually believe in.

segments.speaker: Warren Carpenter
segments.text: You lied! You're a liar! You're a liar!

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Right before this story went to air this week, Kristina Karamo finally agreed to an interview. I reached her while she was taking a morning walk. I asked her about her year in power. I told her it seemed like, for all her good intentions, the party's ended up in disarray, broke, and ineffective, without the money it needs to win elections next year.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: I will say, I reject your premise that my tenure should be defined by funds. See, that's the problem. Your premise is off. Your premise is that I should be defined by money, because the only people that benefit from the premise you're positing is the political class. The only people that benefit are the elitists. And I was elected to reject that premise.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: This is what it's like to talk to her about this. She wouldn't say what she'd do to get the party out of this mess. She wouldn't even acknowledge that they're in a mess.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: We're not bankrupt. That's not true. So the thing about it is, we are operating at a positive cash flow. So yes, it has-- have I hit the financial goals that I would like? Not at the level I would like, but we are on our way.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Well, that's why I guess I'm asking just for any example. Is there a fundraiser in which you tapped into businesses that had been sitting on the sidelines, like you talked about in your campaign?

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: Of course.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Or something like that?

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: Of course.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Just any specific you can give me?

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: Yeah, well, for one, yes. But I don't know what specific you're looking for. Because my question is, why are you so dogmatic on the notion of people who want to push the elitist narrative? That's my question. Because I've answered it multiple times.

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: But my question to you, so why are you so aggressive on that notion? I'm not going to go through the nuts and bolts of every person who's given $1 or $10,000 or $20,000 to our administration. I've answered, we're operating at a positive cash flow.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: As of last month, they're bringing in more than they're spending. Not because of any fundraising. They got a payout from a national committee. But they're still deep in debt, and I could not get any specifics from Kristina on how the party would bring in the millions they've always used to run elections for 2024.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: She pointed out, again and again, that was the wrong question. They've cut costs. They do have a plan to run a ground game. And once that happens, I can judge how that goes.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Over the last few months, I've watched her circle of supporters get smaller. District chairs have resigned. Members of the budget committee resigned, upset about the finances and that the leadership wouldn't listen to them. For all intents and purposes, the party split in two.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: What does it feel like to have all these people, who you guys were on the same team to begin with, calling for your ouster or coming after you, making all these claims? Like, what does it feel like? What's the experience like for you?

segments.speaker: Kristina Karamo
segments.text: It's betrayal. I don't like it. But when you realize, again, the fact that our country is corrupt and the way it is, because most of the people involved in politics are dishonest. People want to lie and try to demean my character. I mean, so be it. I just keep going.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I was talking to Jon Smith, who was there when this all began. I said, it seems like the year of Kristina Karamo has been a year of failure. The party stopped doing most of the basic normal stuff any political party has to do.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And they're limping as they go into this major presidential election year. And Jon was like, no. Don't write your story like it was a waste. It wasn't a waste. Things are going to continue to be different now.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: We did something. We changed the party. We put a non-billionaire in charge here. This is just a first step. Maybe a misstep, but we're not going to just disappear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Zoe Chace.

segments.text: You know, I invited him to Hanukkah this year. I don't know. I think it's the last time. He lit the candles. He's great at the dreidel game. But he just kept saying the same thing over and over.

segments.speaker: Ali Hossein
segments.text: Do you take Jesus Christ as your Lord and Savior?
